content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) and its associated comorbidities, titled Module 6: Tuberculosis and Comorbidities. These guidelines are available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-008700-2 and 978-92-4-008701-9. The publication is copyrighted by WHO in 2024, and under the terms of the license, the content can be copied, redistributed, and adapted for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation, and the original English version remains the authoritative edition. Globally, tuberculosis remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, being one of the leading causes of death due to an infectious agent. Five major health-related risk factors—diabetes mellitus, HIV, smoking, undernutrition, and alcohol use disorders—collectively account for nearly half of all new TB cases worldwide. These risk factors are reported annually in WHO’s Global Tuberculosis Report. For the purposes of these guidelines, a health-related risk factor is defined as a condition or action that increases the risk of developing TB disease. Other notable risk factors include silicosis and drug use disorders. When these risk factors occur in individuals with TB, they are considered comorbidities, which can lead to poor treatment outcomes, reduced quality of life, and other adverse health or social consequences, such as increased financial burdens or TB-associated disabilities. The impact of these risk factors varies between and within countries. People with TB often experience additional comorbidities, including pulmonary and mental health conditions, as well as viral hepatitis. Furthermore, TB patients may develop chronic lung disease or other impairments, such as musculoskeletal or neurological impairments, which require specialized care or rehabilitation during and after TB treatment. Addressing these health-related risk factors and comorbidities necessitates holistic, people-centered care within the framework of universal health coverage. Managing individual comorbidities, multimorbidity, TB-associated disabilities, and health-related risk factors is a critical component of the WHO End TB Strategy, which emphasizes integrated, patient-centered care and prevention. The End TB Strategy highlights the importance of routinely assessing and managing relevant comorbidities and health-related risk factors to improve TB treatment outcomes and overall health. The 2023 United Nations High-Level Meeting on TB reaffirmed the global commitment to ending the TB epidemic by 2030, in alignment with the Sustainable Development Goals. Member States pledged to integrate services for TB, HIV, and other comorbidities within primary healthcare systems and to strengthen coordination and collaboration between programs to ensure universal access to integrated prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for TB, HIV, and other comorbidities. They also committed to achieving three key targets by 2027: reaching at least 90% of people who develop TB with quality-assured diagnosis and treatment, providing preventive treatment to at least 90% of individuals at high risk of developing TB (including approximately 15 million people living with HIV), and ensuring that all TB patients have access to health and social benefit packages to prevent financial hardship due to their illness. The WHO consolidated guidelines on TB and comorbidities aim to provide evidence-based recommendations to address TB and its associated comorbidities. These guidelines consolidate the latest recommendations developed by various Guideline Development Groups (GDGs) convened by WHO, which utilized the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach to assess the quality of evidence and formulate recommendations. The GRADE approach rates the certainty of evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low and determines the strength of recommendations as either strong or conditional. The guidelines are accompanied by an operational handbook that provides practical guidance for implementing these recommendations at the country level. Additionally, the guidelines align with WHO’s Framework for Collaborative Action on TB and Comorbidities, which outlines mechanisms for establishing and strengthening collaborative efforts across disease programs and sectors outside the health system to deliver people-centered care for TB and comorbidities. The consolidated guidelines are a living document, with sections progressively updated and added. The first edition focuses on HIV-associated TB, while the second edition will include a section on nutrition. The guidelines aim to support Member States in implementing effective, people-centered interventions to address TB and comorbidities, reduce disease burden, morbidity, and mortality, and alleviate financial hardship for those affected. They also aim to strengthen linkages with national coordination platforms and mechanisms for the Multisectoral Accountability Framework for TB (MAF-TB) to ensure a comprehensive response to TB and its comorbidities. The guidelines were developed under the coordination of Annabel Baddeley, Anna Carlqvist, and Kerri Viney, with guidance from Farai Mavhunga and overall direction from Tereza Kasaeva, Director of the WHO Global Tuberculosis Programme. Contributions were also made by WHO staff and consultants from the Global HIV, Hepatitis, and STIs Programmes. The update was funded by grants from the United States Agency for International Development and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
